Northern Ireland's friendly double-header against Greece will be live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website

Tuesday, 18 July 2023 was the last time Northern Ireland Women played a friendly.

Under interim manager Gail Redmond, NI produced a fine display to beat Czech Republic 2-0 in Opava.

Just over three and a half years later, Northern Ireland will have not one but two friendly fixtures, with Michael McArdle's side taking on Greece in an Inver Park double-header on 27 November and 1 December.

A lot has changed for NI since that last friendly, but, having two pressure-free games finally offers McArdle an opportunity to experiment with tactics and personnel as they take the first step towards building for Euro 2029 qualifying.

Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies

Greece were beaten by England in the first round of the World Cup play-offs

Only eight players who were in the squad for that friendly win are in the current crop over three years on.

Rebecca McKenna, Rebecca Holloway and Simone Magill started while Lauren Wade, Kerry Beattie and Joely Andrews came off the bench.

Fi Morgan and Chloe McCarron were unused substitutes.

Goalkeeper Lilie Woods made her debut, Marissa Callaghan captained the side and Sarah McFadden and Beattie scored the goals in a rare away win.

A month after that friendly victory, Tanya Oxtoby arrived to take over as Kenny Shiels' permanent successor.

She eventually left to take over at Newcastle United in November 2025 and all 26 of her games as NI manager were competitive fixtures.

The introduction of the Nations League and its close ties to Euro and World Cup qualification admittedly left little room in what is now a stacked international women's calendar for friendly games.

During Oxtoby's tenure, NI had two Nations League campaigns sandwiched between Euro 2025 qualifiers.

After falling to Iceland in their Nations League promotion/relegation play off last October, they opted against seeking any friendlies at the end of November as they looked for a successor to Oxtoby.

The competitive games kept coming and Kris Lindsay was then in interim charge of NI's first two 2027 World Cup qualifiers before McArdle took over in April for the four remaining group games and the subsequent first-round play-off defeat against Portugal.

With NI not involved in the second round of the World Cup play-offs while many others are in the upcoming window, McArdle has decided to get the squad together for two friendlies.

With such a young squad at his disposal and with McArdle still relatively new to the job, he is relishing the chance to have the players in camp for an extended period and for NI to test themselves against decent opposition.

"We don't want friendly games in this window, we want to be in the play-offs but we had planned for both [scenarios], this has been a long-term plan," he said.

"Greece I specifically selected because I knew we couldn't draw them in the Nations League as we're in the same pot, but also they're a strong nation who are progressing well and are close to ourselves in the rankings.

"They'll be a real test for us. It was very deliberate selection."

Northern Ireland suffered a 7-1 aggregate defeat in the first round World Cup play-off against Portugal

McArdle wants NI to be "more horrible to play against" and feels they will work on that in this camp as well as what they do when in possession to trouble opponents.

Greece, like Northern Ireland, exited the World Cup play-offs at the first round after an aggregate 8-1 defeat to England.

They had been in good form before back-to-back defeats by the Lionesses, winning five games this year as they topped Group C4 to seal promotion to League B.

"It gives us two games to try and win first and foremost because we need to develop the winning mentality, but also to test some things because a lot of the identity and how we play, after six competitive games, there is still work to do particularly in possession, we've not quite done that yet," McArdle continued.

"That identity that we never give up and are constantly going, that is the case for the group, but we have to improve the athleticism and the duels to bridge the gap to qualification to tournaments."

Qualifying for the 2029 Euros in Germany does not begin until 2028, but McArdle's side have a testing Nations League campaign to prepare for next year.

They have been drawn against Poland, Finland and Belarus and the Scot revealed that he is already planning ahead for potential friendly opponents for next year's November/December international window to maximise time spent with his squad if they are not in the Nations League play-offs.

"There's also the importance of taking all the activity available to us and that's crucial for us growing and moving forward.

"We're already planning for next November/December window and selecting opponents because there is a deliberate strategy how we evolve the group.

"Part of that is strategically picking opponents which will help us grow. The friendlies, in a sense it's not competitive games, but we'll approach them in the same way."

MN202611_sw68w6y6as.t:
Kansas City Current, who were formed in 2020, won this year's National Women's Soccer League championship

"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."

Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.

The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (£229).

Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.

Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.

It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.

Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.

So what is behind the explosion in popularity?

And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?

The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.

The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.

"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.

"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."

While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.

The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.

There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.

As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.

Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.

Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.

"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.

"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."

It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.

But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.

"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.

"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."

Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move

Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium

Washington Spirit's Trinity Rodman benefited from a NWSL decision in December 2025 to lift the league's salary cap for a 'High Impact Player'

Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.

Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.

International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.

"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.

"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."

Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.

In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.

On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.

As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."

"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.

"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again.

Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma

Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal machine Khadija Shaw and most of England's double European Championship-winning squad for example.

Amercian stars such as Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma at Chelsea, and Manchester City's Sam Coffey, have also swapped the US for the WSL in the past two years.

Broadcaster Oatley, who has been covering women's football since the 2005 World Cup, is keen for such players to be more visible off the pitch.

"I would love to see WSL players on mainstream TV shows, podcasts, social media platforms, not just on women's football programmes where the audience already knows everything about them," she says.

"It would not be for everyone, but for those who are comfortable, who have the biggest personalities, I think we could use that much more to grow our audience."

Oatley has been covering NWSL games for the past four seasons and she believes US clubs have mastered putting on events.

"When you're trying to promote a product in sport, you can't guarantee the team is going to play well and win," she says.

"But you can ensure the people who come to the game have a great experience.

"I love the enthusiasm, the positivity, the vibe of 'let's make this big'. It's a brilliant experience."

It is a balance the WSL wrestles with. With attendances plateauing this season, questions have arisen around its target audience and whether to market matches such as the north London derby between Tottenham and Arsenal as a rivalry or a family-friendly event.

Oatley's perspective is that it ought to be both, while recognising the different challenges in this country.

"I didn't understand that criticism," she says, "because they weren't saying: 'Only come to this game if you're a family'. It was being promoted all round.

"I don't think it's one size fits all marketing wise - the main thing is awareness."

The NWSL Fan Fest at The Wharf in Washington DC was part of a series of events around the championship game on Saturday

It is a challenge the NWSL has embraced, and seen attendances rise accordingly.

"We want to ensure that we provided a big enough tent where everyone can feel welcome and included, whether they're there for the rivalries and the competitive tactics, or they're experiencing it for the first time," says Jones Simmer.

"To grow the sport, all fans need to be able to come to an NWSL game and have a great experience."

This season, league finalists Current and Spirit played at a remarkable 17 different times between them, reflecting the four timezones and vast nature of the USA.

It is all part of the country's sporting landscape, but given the WSL's continued conundrum about fixture scheduling, it is interesting that NWSL supporters manage to find the matches regardless.

"I have a lot of sympathy with schedulers because men's football got there first," Oakley says.

"Maybe the solution is deciding certain time slots are for women's football and sticking with them."

It does not appear the growth in the NWSL will slow down any time soon.

The Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer will feature the USA as one of the favourites and women's soccer will feature at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028.

The US will also host the 2031 Women's World Cup.

"It is amazing how the NWSL is cracking into culture," Jones Simmer says.

"We get excited about these catalytic opportunities to expand the community engagement, awareness and relevance of the NWSL."

Shelly Magee and Clinton McKeever had hoped their son would be born in Newry

A couple who are expecting their first child have said their excitement has turned "into complete worry" because of the suspension of maternity services at their local hospital.

Shelly Magee was due to give birth in Newry's Daisy Hill Hospital in January but from Monday, the Southern Trust is moving all hospital-based births to Craigavon.

Her partner, Clinton McKeever, said they are now dreading the much longer journey from their home in Mullaghbawn to Craigavon in the middle of winter.

The trust announced the temporary suspension of maternity services at Daisy Hill in September , saying it had been unable to recruit enough consultant obstetricians to maintain a safe service for both mums and babies.

From Monday, it has advised all expectant mothers in the Southern Health Trust to go to Craigavon Area Hospital - not Daisy Hill - for all labour and birthing services, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynaecology support.

The trust said an estimated 13 women could possibly deliver their babies on Monday at Craigavon.

That includes planned C sections and those booked in for induction - four of these had originally planned to have their babies in Daisy Hill.

Woman says 40-mile journey to hospital while having contractions was 'scary'

'My son might not have survived without Daisy Hill maternity service'

No babies to be born at hospital from end of November

It added that patients will receive the same high standard of care from experienced specialists, including staff from Daisy Hill who are relocating to Craigavon.

But the expectant couple have not been reassured by the trust's statements.

Magee said Craigavon Area Hospital is "50 minutes from the house" by car but her partner pointed out that could rise to 90 minutes in heavy traffic or severe weather.

"A child doesn't choose a time to come," McKeever told BBC News NI.

"To strip away a maternity service and claim it's for the safety of women is scandalous... there's no thought of safety in that journey."

He said he was speaking from experience, having "had a taste of the journey already in a scenario that would be considered a crisis".

About five years ago, his father was badly injured in a fall during which he suffered several broken ribs and a punctured lung.

McKeever drove his father to Craigavon, having been advised by their local health clinic that it would take too long for an ambulance to get to Mullaghbawn.

"The traffic was crazy and he felt every bump - I felt guilty for every bump. I got him there in the end but it was a very, very stressful journey," he recalled.

"To know that I have to do it again with Shelly here, it's very concerning. It's took the excitement out of the whole thing and turned it into complete worry."

To avoid having to drive to Craigavon in active labour in early January the couple are now considering booking a hotel or rented accommodation near the hospital.

Despite their concerns, they were full of praise for midwives who cared for them in Newry and Crossmaglen, acknowledging staff also face uncertainty.

"They're brilliant, they keep up with everything, but they're in the dark as much as we are, that's the frustrating thing," Magee said.

The trust apologised to women who had planned to give birth at Daisy Hill Hospital

Hospital campaigners have also raised concerns about what the trust is describing as a temporary suspension.

Conor Patterson, chair of the Daisy Hill Future Group, expressed "deep concern" that the move would affect "time-critical access to maternity care".

He claimed it subjects families in counties Down, Armagh and the border area to "life and death risks".

"Moving up to 1,800 births from Newry to Craigavon risks not just destabilising Craigavon's maternity unit but will threaten also its ability to safely provide other acute medical services."

According to figures from the trust, 1,713 babies were born at Daisy Hill last year, while Craigavon dealt with 2,768 births.

When asked how Craigavon will deal with hundreds of extra births each year, the trust said it was continuing efforts to secure consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill. There are also plans to open an additional ward.

It said it was also preparing continuity arrangements to temporarily consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon from Monday.

The trust employs 15 consultant obstetricians. However, sickness, reduced working hours and maternity leave means not all 15 can contribute to the on-call rota.

Despite ongoing recruitment efforts across the UK and internationally, the trust said it has been unable to recruit enough consultants to maintain a safe and reliable service at both hospitals.

Its spokesperson said inpatient maternity care at Craigavon had been identified as the safest and most sustainable arrangement for maintaining the trust's services.

The number of midwives employed within the maternity units at both acute hospitals has dropped from pre-pandemic levels.

In October 2019, there were 55.6 midwives employed on a full-time basis at Daisy Hill Hospital and 95.04 full-time in Craigavon.

As of last month, that had dropped to 47.57 midwives at Daisy Hill and 82.58 in Craigavon.

However, the trust said midwifery care has changed over the past seven years, with more midwives now working in the community.

The trust added that 16 newly-appointed midwives are due to start work between November 2026 and January 2027.

Its medical director for maternity and women's health, Dr Beverley Adams, said all efforts had been made to avoid the suspension and she apologised for any disappointment caused for women who had planned to give birth at Daisy Hill.

"Teams at both hospitals have been working hard to manage these challenges and prepare to provide all births, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynae care for the Southern Trust at Craigavon Area hospital."

A spokesperson for the trust said that of the 1,088 planned births up to the end of February, it estimated that 294 of these were originally planned for Daisy Hill.

A proportion of these women may already have been referred to Craigavon based on risk.

To support the maternity service at Craigavon, a total of 37 staff, including midwives and sisters, are to transfer.

It is not the first time that Daisy Hill has lost hospital services because of staffing problems.

Its emergency general surgery was permanently moved to Craigavon in 2024 , two years after it was temporarily suspended due to recruitment challenges.

The truth will set you free, so goes the saying. In the case of the Democratice Republica of Congo (DRC), this is literally true. With Some Western observers beginning to openly acknowledge that the roots of the DRC crisis are in the country itself, could Congolese find the courage to admit the truth that will free their nation?

In an article for the Washington Examiner , American academic and erstwhile Presidential advisor, Michael Rubin, explicity spelt out what few Western commentators, journalists, academics will have either the courage, or it seems integrity to say.

“The only reason to side with the Democratic Republic of Congo” the article announced unabashedly, “is corruption.” DRC, corruption, tell me something I don’t know, might be any informed reader’s reaction. But such a reaction would be hasty. While not much fo what Ruben says is new, what is new, is that he addresse a number of truths that many assiduously ignore.

President Donald Trump may have dismissed African countries, in his now familiar less than refined way, as “sh**hole countries,” said Ruben, but “credit where credit is due…his his team has paid more attention to Central Africa, than almost any administration before it.”

The compliment however carries a sting in the tail. Ruben immediately goes on to point out that “while the Statement Department and special envoy Massad Boulos present their engagement as a quest for peace, trade looms large.”

That, Ruben hastens to add, is not a band thing in itself, but an alert reader will have concluded that while of course, trade engagement might be welcome, it is nonetheless less than desirable that what pretends to be an engagement for peace, should be about nothing more than trade.

And some Africans (although admittedly not many, perhaps a handful out of a billion, certainly not among Congolese) might also add that attention from America is not necessarilly a good thing, but that is another story of African woes.

Ruben goes to explain the reason for the Trump administration’s close attention.

“The Democratic Republic of Congo is believed to hold some $24 trillion in rare earths and strategic metals underground. In theory, the DRC could be to the 21 st Century economy what Saudi Arabia, with its vast oil reserves, was to the 20 th Centure.”

The inference is clear. What is presented as engagement for peace, is simply about resource extraction. And what Ruben leaves unsaid, is that the quest for peace is at best an afterthought, if not an irrelevance. As long as Congo’s Felix Tshisekedi, continues to open the door to the unbridled extraction of his country’s natural resources, he can consider himself a protected species, however destructive to the environment that species may be.

But Ruben gets more forthright. “In 2016, President Joseph Kabila agreed not to seek a third term, paving the way for the DRC’s first democratic transition. The optimism was misplaced,” he writes, “Observers concluded that Felix Tshisekedi had lost to Martin Fayulu, but last minute manoeuvring and bribes secured Tshisekedi’s election. Tshisekedi’s record is dismal. While Rubio [US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio], blames Rwanda for the instability in the Eastern DRC, he glosses over some uncomfortable truths.”

“First, Rwanda and the DRC cooperated on shared security until Tshisekedi, with nothing else to build his election campaign on, turned to ethnic incitement. Second, despite all the the talk about the Rwanda army in Eastern DRC, none of Rwanda’s accusers has been able to produce a single Rwandan prisoner of war, let alone a body.”

“In fact, the State Department seems to be playing into Tshisekedi’s racism by assuming that every Tutsi…is Rwandan, even though more than half a million Tutsi live in Congo.”

Ruben goes on to break what for many in the Western commentators remains a taboo, dare to tell the truth about the rebel AFC/M23.

“Third, the idea that the M23 rebel group [AFC/M23 now renamed FRN], is illegitimate is also false. M23 formed to force the DRC government to honour its previous commitments to reform. In 2024, I crossed the border clandestinely from Uganda and spent a week with M23, having already spent time in Kinshasa, the DRC’s capital.”

“What I saw was impressive: more food, greater security, more public works, and a general sense of optimism and multiethnic inclusion. There is a reaon the DRC cannot defeat M23, and it has nothing to do with its army. When M23 ambushes Blackwater mercenaries and massacres them, Congolese people applaud. Unfortunately, in pursuit of contracts, Boulos has sought shortcuts, each more self defeating than the last.”

There is much to unpick there. Ruben could have gone farther, much farther. That even the little he has acknowledged seems quite extraordinary, shames every other Western commentator, journalist, human rights group and academic.

There is not a time when Rwanda has not called for the acknowledgement of the underlying causes of the DRC crisis, and there is not a time when Western commentators have not only intransigently looked away from those facts, have studiously distorted them, to point fingers at Rwanda.

There has been an unwritten conspiracy among Western commentators, when commeting on the DRC crisis, a conspiracy has included journalists. It is for instance undeniable that governance quickly returns to areas controlled by AFC/M23 as was, FRN as it is now called. Children can go to school, there is more food, because people can return to their farms. Life begins again.

But ask any Western journalist, academic or commentator, and they will regale you with “human rights abuses” by AFC/M23. The same journalists, academics, and commentators, who never saw or heard of the wholesale murders, rape, pillaging, including the burning of human beings alive and cannibalising them, in the same areas, before the rebel group occupied them, suddenly see human rights abuses, when the perpetrators of such horrors are defeated and life returns to normal.

And Ruben could indeed have gone even farther; it is a calumny on the AFC/M23 to say they “massacred” the mercenaries. That is what the Congolese army, FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) coalition does. AFC/M23 rebels observe the Geneva convention as they do the protection of civilians. Massacres are committed by the Congolese army, FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo), and its coalition.

And no wonder, it is a coalition that includes the so called Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group formed by the planners and perpetrators of the 1994 Genocide Against Tutsi in Rwanda, the so called Wazalendo, a collection of formerly murderous armed groups roaming throughout the DRC, now anointed by the state as “patriots” even more heavily armed, largely under the command of the FDLR. These are reinforced by Burundi forces, 20,000 or so of them are now in the DRC, and of course, the mercenaries.

Every soldier of fortune it seems is now in the DRC. Eric Prince, a favourite of the Trump administration, has his Blackwater group there, joined by South Americans, and on the periphery, various individuals from some African states, all in contravention of every international and African Union convention on mercenaries. Yet Western academics, journalists, commentators, human rights groups, shrug and look the other way, to point fingers at Rwanda.

But it may be a little ungracious to imply that Ruben leaves out too much because he does not say all that he might. The truths he does tell are unvarnished, without fear or favour, where other Western commentators strain to conceal them.

“Tshisekedi is limited to two terms” Ruben reminds us, “but Boulos indulges his fantasy of a third term. That might work in an ordinary dictatorship, but Tshiskedi does not control Kinshasa, let alone mines more than a thousand miles away. The DRC is also among the most courrupt countries in the world. In practical terms, that means no contract is sacred…”

In otherwords, in trying to flatter Tshisekedi, Massad Boulos is deceiving both himself and Tshisekedi. The truth he suggests, would serve America better.

“That is why good governance matters. As Rubio sanctions Rwanda, he forgets that no American sanctions could compare to the genocide that American indifference helped make possible. He is merely pushing away one of the most stable and potentially most pro American governments. Efforts to preserve Tshisekedi are also backfiring on their authors in another way. Rubio and Boulos embrace Tshisekedi as a dictator they can do business with, but his incompetence and unpopularity are hastening the security collapse.”

Good governance does indeed matter, but Ruben knows that at no time has the West ever cared about good governance in Africa. For the West, good governance is synonimous with “pro West” and without the “pro West” good governance is not acknowledged. Citing Rwanda, as pro West, is simplistic.

The RPF (Rwanda Patriotic Front) leadership in Rwanda, has a clear political philosophy, that is rooted in what is best for Rwanda and Rwandans. While the West still sees African states satellites that serve Western interests, the RPF believes that Rwanda, should play its part in the world, make friends and true partnerships that are mutually beneficial.

But in his own way, albeit perhaps inadvertently, Ruben goes on to highlight that very thing. That seeing Africa, in this case Congo, as nothing more than a gaping mine is in the last analysis counterproductive.

“Kabila, remembered for allowing a transition, is now leading a military offensive to redraw Congo. Rather than bringing peace, Trump’s or Boulos’s quest for contracts now threatens to reignite the war. Africa is complex, and American engagement is welcome. But Trump, Rubio, and Boulos’s unreserved support for the DRC makes little sense unless corruption is influencing decision-making and greed is overriding an objective assessment of American interests, American influence, and the DRC’s future.”

For any engaged African, this is stating the obvious, so much so, it is no longer worth reiterating. The same could have been said of the Americans and Mobutu, as many other Western factotums around Africa.

Coming from an American commentator, however, especially one who has served as a Presidential adviser, these are stunning acknowledgements, whose importance cannot be overstated. His conclusion is nonetheless instructive. Even he, cannot see, or will not see the DRC through any other lens than how it might best serve Western interests.

“The DRC matters” Ruben concludes, “but they way to secure its place in the global economy and gain access to its rare earths is to push Tshisekedi into exile or prison, adopt a zero tolerance policy toward ethnic incitement, and demand that Kinshasa follow Kigali’s example, by transforming itself into an economic powerhouse.”

Africans should be wary of the word complex, whenever and wherever it is employed in reference to them. It is almost always imperial code that acknowledging the self evident facts would not serve imperialistic interests. How many times have Western commentators setentiously declared that the DRC crisis is “complex” even as they strenuously draw attention away from the root causes of that crisis?

“The DRC matters” Ruben says. Yes, but to whom? And why? Seen from his persective, it matters to the West, because of its rare earths, and whatever must be done, must be done to best achieve Western ends.

The Congolese, the region and Africa in general, needs must see it differently. The DRC matters as an entity that must serve its people. Its economy must be national before it is global, to paraphrase a common aphorism, it must serve locally to matter globally. It must be rid of Tshisekedi, have zero tolerance for corruption, for its own sake, not to better serve American or Western interests.

That, would be the example of Rwanda, which looks to its people first, then stretches out the hand of friendship to the world. The distinction may seem subtle but it is a difference between a ntion that has a sense of itself, and one that lacks an identity, existing only because it is useful for others.

The importance of Ruben’s intervention, as a rare acknowledgement of the facts by a Western commentator, cannot be overemphasized, but he must be read differently, depending on whether the reader’s interest lies in seeing the DRC become a nation that is self aware, and looks at itself from its own perspective, or become just a more efficient an entity that exists to serve others’ interests.

Vincent Gasana is a Senior Editorial Lead at Kigali Today Ltd. He spent many years at the BBC. He regularly write for KT Press

A similar 24-hour strike took place on Friday as part of the same pay dispute

Consultants and specialist doctors have begun a 24-hour strike as part of an ongoing dispute over pay.

It follows a separate 24-hour strike on Friday in which resident doctors took industrial action as part of the same dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

The strike will take action in the form of Christmas Day cover meaning full emergency cover will remain in place

The strike, which will begin on at 07:00 GMT, will take action in the form of Christmas Day cover meaning full emergency cover will remain in place.

Butler said: "My door remains open but, to be clear, going beyond the 3.5% as recommended by the independent pay review body would have significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce."

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Dr David Farren of the BMA said nothing meaningful had risen from meeting with the health minster about pay disputes

Dr David Farren, chair of of the British Medical Association's (BMA) Northern Ireland consultants committee told Good Morning Ulster that doctors are "not being valued in northern Ireland".

"We have given the trusts a six week notice period, which is six times longer than the legal requirement, so they can plan for that.

"No doctor wishes to strike, we are incredibly sorry that it has come to this."

He advised the public that "full emergency cover will remain in place."

What will be affected however will be "hospital appointments, routine investigations, routine operating lists", he said.

Dr Farren added that the official advice is that "if you have not been notified, you go ahead to your appointment.

"However don't be surprised if your appointment doesn't happen when you get there."

He added that the BMA gave the health trusts "a six week notice period, which is six times longer than the legal requirement, so they can plan for that."

"We met with the minster on 1 October, any sort of meaningful engagement could've halted these strikes, after that meeting we heard nothing."

The health minister said Monday's strike, paired with Friday's will have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery, with around 1,694 patients expected to be impacted".

He also warned that "there will be further consequences for patients as we head into the busy winter period due to the knock-on effect of the strikes as we reschedule cancelled activity".

The health minster told Good Morning Ulster that the proposed pay rise would equate to "around £280m".

He said his "real pressure" was trying to deliver the Real Living Wage for domiciliary care workers, "there are many woman out there delivering care packages at home and my ambition is to give them the Real Living Wage," he said.

"I will talk to anybody, in any place about this," he said.

Ahavuye isanamu, Présidence du Conseil du Togo/X

Perezida wa Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (RDC), Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi, na mugenzi we wa Kenya, William Ruto, bumvikanye ku kongera kubaka umubano wa dipolomasi hagati y'ibihugu byombi, wari umaze igihe urangwamo umwuka mubi.

Ibyo babiganiriyeho ku cyumweru, tariki ya 22 Ugushyingo (11) 2026, mu nama y'abakuru b'ibihugu bine yabereye i Oyo muri Repubulika ya Congo, yahuje RDC, Kenya, Repubulika ya Congo na Togo.

Iyi nama yatumijwe na Perezida wa Repubulika ya Congo, Denis Sassou-N'Guesso, yitabirwa kandi na Faure Gnassingbé, Perezida w'inama y'abaminisitiri ya Togo akaba n'umuhuza w'Umuryango wa Afurika Yunze Ubumwe (AU) mu bibazo by'umutekano mu burasirazuba bwa RDC.

Mu itangazo ryasohowe nyuma y'iyi nama, RDC na Kenya byatangaje ko byiyemeje gusubizaho byuzuye umubano wa dipolomasi, harimo no gusubizaho ba ambasaderi b'ibihugu byombi.

Mu butumwa yashyize ku rubuga rwa X, Perezida William Ruto yavuze ko yagiranye ibiganiro na Perezida Tshisekedi, bemeranya gutangiza indi ntangiriro y'umubano w'ibihugu byabo ishingiye ku bwizerane, kubahana no gufatanya.

Yongeyeho ko impande zombi zemeranyije kongera gushyiraho ibikorwa bya Komisiyo ihuriweho ishinzwe ubufatanye (Joint Grand Commission for Cooperation), kongera ibiganiro bya dipolomasi no gushimangira ubufatanye mu bucuruzi, iterambere ry'ubukungu, umutekano n'umuco.

Ibi biganiro bibaye nyuma y'igihe umubano wa Nairobi na Kinshasa utifashe neza, cyane cyane kuva mu Ukuboza (12) 2023, ubwo RDC yagaragazaga kutishimira kuba ihuriro rya AFC, rifitanye isano n'umutwe wa M23, ryaratangirijwe muri Kenya. Ibyo byakurikiwe no guhamagaza ambasaderi wa RDC wari i Nairobi.

Mu bindi byemeranyijweho, abayobozi bombi bongeye gushimangira ko bazubahiriza amahame agenga umubano w'ibihugu, arimo kubaha ubusugire bw'ibihugu, kutivanga mu bibazo by'imbere mu kindi gihugu, kubana neza no gukemura amakimbirane binyuze mu nzira z'amahoro.

Ku rwego rw'ubukungu, biyemeje kongera ubufatanye mu bucuruzi no gushishikariza ishoramari hagati y'ibihugu byombi.

Mu rwego rw'ubuzima, RDC na Kenya byemeranyije kongera ubufatanye mu gukumira no kurwanya icyorezo cya Ebola, kikomeje kuba kimwe mu bibazo by'ubuzima rusange bisaba ubufatanye bw'ibihugu byo mu karere.

Iyi nama ibaye mu gihe akarere k'Ibiyaga Bigari gakomeje gushakirwa ibisubizo birambye by'ibibazo by'umutekano, cyane cyane intambara n'umutekano muke mu burasirazuba bwa RDC, aho Kinshasa ikunze kubishinja u Rwanda, ariko narwo rukabihakana.

Kongera kubaka umubano hagati ya RDC na Kenya bishobora gufungura indi nzira y'ubufatanye mu bucuruzi, dipolomasi n'umutekano, mu gihe impande zombi zizashyira mu bikorwa ibyo zumvikanyeho.

The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila , in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

Ian Holloway surpassed 1,000 games managing in English football during his time at Swindon

Manager Ian Holloway has been sacked by Swindon Town after just over two years in charge.

The Robins' 2-0 loss at Newport County on Saturday left them 17th in League Two and was their fourth successive defeat in all competitions - conceding 10 goals in the process.

They have won only two of their past 15 matches, and Holloway last month described himself as a "dead man walking" if Swindon's form did not turn around.

"Since joining the club towards the end of 2024, Ian has played an important role in stabilising our on-field position and helping the club make progress season upon season," read a Swindon statement.

Swindon's Holloway labels himself dead man walking

Lewis double fires County to victory against Swindon

"However, following careful consideration of recent results and performances, the club believes that now is the right time to take a different direction.

"This has not been an easy decision, but the board firmly believes that it is important to make difficult decisions when necessary, always with the best interests of Swindon Town at heart."

Coaches Gavin Gunning and Steve Mildenhall will take charge of the first team on an interim basis, with David Carney assisting them.

Holloway was appointed in October 2024 until the end of that season, with Swindon one place above the relegation zone.

He surpassed 1,000 games managing in English football two months later and signed a two-year contract in March 2025, having steered Swindon into play-off contention.

Promotion was the aim last season, with Holloway issuing a rallying call at the start of the campaign for Swindon to be the "team I believe we can" be.

They were in the automatic promotion spots in February, but only three wins in their last 13 games, including a 2-1 defeat by Chesterfield in a must-win final match, meant they missed out on the play-offs.

Although Swindon won three of their first five league games this season, they are without a win in their past five and have scored one goal in that time.

Ian Holloway was ushered away by stewards after approaching Swindon's fans after Saturday's loss at Newport County

Andrew Hawes, BBC Radio Wiltshire Swindon Town commentator

This season has largely consisted of feeling Swindon are two games away from a crisis and Australia-based chairman Clem Morfuni's arrival in the country to see deserved defeats by Newport and Grimsby finally made it one.

The team have consistently struggled to create goals and chances despite having League Two's player of the year Aaron Drinan, a rare exception to a chronic injury list.

The fans' energy for Holloway had grown thin, and sometimes vice versa.

Being ushered away by a steward at Rodney Parade as his last act may be a summary of how both felt about each other.

But there is a clear feel of stagnation at Swindon - and that means putting another manager on the chopping block is no guarantee of improvement.

An earlier graduation at the University of Global Health Equity (UGHE), one of the international entities in Rwanda

KIGALI – Women now make up the majority of students enrolled in Rwanda’s tertiary education institutions, overtaking men in a reversal of the situation recorded seven years earlier, according to latest data by the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR).

In Rwanda, tertiary education refers to learning after secondary school. It covers universities, polytechnics, colleges and other higher learning institutions offering qualifications ranging from diplomas and advanced diplomas to Bachelor’s, Master’s and doctoral degrees.

The finding therefore goes beyond university enrolment alone.

The Measuring Gender-in-Trade Statistics – Country Report: Rwanda , released last week shows that women accounted for 51.8 per cent of tertiary-level students in 2024, compared with 48.2 per cent for men.

The shift comes as Rwanda’s higher education system continues to expand.

The Ministry of Education’s 2024/25 Education Statistical Yearbook records 153,318 students enrolled in higher education institutions in the academic year ending July 2025, up from 130,474 the previous year.

The gender figures mark a reversal from 2017, when men accounted for 53.4 per cent of tertiary students, while women made up 46.6 per cent.

Earlier enrolment figures also show that men had a clear numerical lead at the beginning of the decade.

By 2024, however, women had moved ahead, accounting for more than half of all students in tertiary-level institutions, according to the NISR report.

The report also points to a similar pattern at secondary level, where women accounted for 55.2 per cent of students in 2024, compared with 44.8 per cent for men.

The change in enrolment comes alongside improvements in women’s literacy. Their literacy rate rose from 60.1 per cent in 2006 to 73.6 per cent in 2024. Men still recorded a higher literacy rate of 78.4 per cent, up from 71.5 per cent over the same period.

The report says women’s growing presence in tertiary education could put them in a stronger position to enter higher-value services and formal trade, including technical and managerial roles.

It projects that the shift could contribute to gender parity in high-skilled trade sectors within five to ten years. But that outcome will depend on whether barriers such as occupational segregation, hiring discrimination and unpaid care responsibilities limit women’s transition from education into employment.

The report recommends tracking the transition of male and female graduates into trade-related jobs, encouraging gender-responsive recruitment and expanding mentorship and leadership opportunities for women.

KIGALI – When a woman in one Rwandan village expressed interest in contesting for a local leadership position, she had the encouragement of her community but faced opposition from her husband.

Despite believing she had the ability to serve, she eventually abandoned her ambition after her husband refused to let her contest.

The experience, shared by Marie Médiatrice Umubyeyi, Executive Secretary of the National Women’s Council (CNF), illustrates how restrictions within households can undermine women’s participation in public life, even as opportunities for their leadership expand.

Umubyeyi said some women are not necessarily afraid of politics but lack support from their spouses, with household expectations and concerns about childcare sometimes standing in the way of their ambitions.

Her account comes as Rwanda renews its local government leadership structures, with women being encouraged to take up positions in district councils and contribute more directly to decisions affecting their communities.

But for women to fully exercise that leadership, CNF says they must also be able to make decisions about their lives, challenge harmful attitudes and speak out against practices that undermine their rights.

During the November 21 elections for councilors, CNF undertook activities aimed at preparing women to participate, including changing mindsets among those who believed politics was not an appropriate space for them.

The council also organized training to help women build confidence, overcome fear and develop public speaking skills.

Umubyeyi argued that women have historically played important roles in governance and should not allow misconceptions about politics to discourage them from seeking leadership positions.

“Women’s participation in governance is essential because, even in the past, people used to say that no king ruled without a queen mother or a queen. All this demonstrates the role women have played in good governance,” she said.

The growing representation of women is already visible in some local government structures. In Huye, women account for 58.8 per cent of the district council, with 10 women among its 17 members following the latest elections.

Three of the eight newly elected councilors are Associate Professor Anne Marie Kagwesage, the outgoing Chairperson of Huye district council, Pauline Kayisire and Médiatrice Mukeshimana, who both served on the outgoing council.

They joined five women councilors elected to represent women, alongside female representatives of the National Women’s Council and youth.

While women’s participation in local governance is expanding, CNF says the attitudes they encounter within their households remain a significant obstacle.

Umubyeyi said some husbands fear that their wives’ participation in local leadership could make them less available at home, leaving household responsibilities and childcare unattended.

She challenged this reasoning, arguing that raising children and managing household responsibilities should be shared between men and women.

“Families should not assume women cannot balance public responsibilities with their roles at home. Where people share responsibilities, the upbringing of children is the responsibility of both the woman and the man,” she said.

She added that preventing a woman from pursuing leadership because of assumptions about her ability to manage family responsibilities can amount to denying her an opportunity to exercise her rights.

“Why don’t you allow someone to go ahead and see whether they can manage the responsibilities you claim they will not be able to balance? You might be surprised that they can handle them,” Umubyeyi said.

For CNF, changing such attitudes is part of a wider effort to ensure that women can exercise their rights without intimidation or restrictions. It is also a message that extends beyond political participation to the fight against gender-based violence.

Breaking the Silence Around Gender-Based Violence

Speaking during a community outreach activity in Gishamvu Sector, Huye district, Aline Umutoni, Director General in the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion (MIGEPROF), urged residents to take an active role in identifying and reporting gender-based violence.

She called on community members not to remain silent when they witness abuse, encouraging them to report cases and use the country’s Isange One Stop Centres, which provide victims with access to medical, psychosocial and legal support.

“We are encouraging residents not to keep quiet when they see violence taking place. Especially during these 16 Days of Activism Against GBV, come to our One Stop Centres and report these crimes,” Umutoni said.

She said community members should not wait for victims to report incidents themselves, but should help alert authorities and ensure those affected receive protection and justice.

“You should be the first respondents to help the authorities avert these crimes and find help and justice for the victims,” she said, adding that the ministry was using different platforms to sustain awareness beyond the annual campaign.

At an earlier community sports activity in Huye, Umutoni also highlighted how silence can affect the handling of sexual abuse cases, particularly those involving children and young people.

She cautioned that delays in reporting sexual violence can compromise the collection of forensic evidence needed for investigations and prosecution, urging victims and those around them to seek assistance as quickly as possible.

Although girls are particularly exposed to sexual harassment and abuse, she noted that boys can also become victims and should equally be encouraged to speak out and seek protection.

Umutoni stressed that preventing gender-based violence requires the involvement of everyone, including families, communities, authorities and individuals. Its effects, she said, extend beyond victims to affect entire households and society.

The 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, observed annually from November 25 to December 10, links the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women with Human Rights Day.

The campaign was established in 1991 to emphasize that violence against women is a human rights violation requiring sustained collective action.

In a contemporary world, women’s empowerment must extend beyond representation in decision-making structures to challenging attitudes that silence women, restrict their choices or prevent them from exercising their rights.

The National Women’s Council (NWC) is continuing its nationwide campaign to promote women’s participation in leadership and decision-making, with activities scheduled across several districts from November 20 to December 30, 2026.

The campaign includes community outreach, radio discussions, school and university engagements, and coverage of women’s elections at village and district levels. Activities are planned in districts including Huye, Nyarugenge, Rwamagana, Gatsibo, Musanze and Ngororero, among others.

Working with the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion (MIGEPROF), local authorities, the Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB), GIZ and Kigali Today, the NWC is also incorporating activities under the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. These include public awareness campaigns in schools, markets and sporting events, highlighting women’s role in development and addressing gender-based violence.

Radio programs, social media campaigns, short films and community meetings will be used to reach wider audiences and showcase women in leadership, business and community development, as well as men who support women’s advancement.

The program demonstrates that the campaign to increase women’s participation in leadership is ongoing, extending beyond elections to sustained public awareness, advocacy and engagement at community level.
